Like I'll start dragging in new frames or typing out my idea right on top of the section they're actively trying to present to the group. 

In the moment, I'm just so pumped up about it. I'm like, "Oh my gosh, this is brilliant, this connects perfectly to what they're saying!" I've had to apologize so many times, like, "Oh my gosh, I'm so sorry, keep going, I just got excited," but I know it gets on people's nerves when we're trying to have a structured meeting and I'm just bulldozing through their turn to speak.

turns.doctor_question: Before age 12, did you often leave your seat when you were supposed to stay seated?
turns.patient_response:
Wait, leaving my seat? Like, getting up in class when I wasn't supposed to? Um... honestly, I don't really think so. I mean, I'm trying to think back to elementary school and middle school, and... no, I don't remember that being a big issue for me. 

Like, I know some kids did that. There was this one boy in my third-grade class, Jason, who literally could not stay in his chair. He was always getting up to sharpen his pencil, or look out the window, or just kind of wander over to the reading corner, and the teacher was constantly telling him to sit back down. But I don't think I ever did that. I mean, I was definitely squirmy in my seat, you know? Like, I'd cross and uncross my legs a million times, or I'd lean all the way back until the front legs of the chair came off the floor—which, actually, I did fall backward once in fifth grade and it made this huge crash and everyone stared at me, which was mortifying. But I wasn't actually getting up and walking around the room. 

I think I was too worried about getting in trouble to actually leave my desk. I was a bit of a rule-follower when it came to the big, obvious rules like "stay in your seat." My way of, I guess, being restless was more about fidgeting with my hands under the desk, or doodling all over the margins of my notebooks, or just completely zoning out and staring at the clock. But physically getting up and leaving my seat during a lesson or when we were supposed to be working? No, I really don't think I did that. Even at home, when I was doing homework, I might have gotten distracted and started playing with my erasers, like I said before, but I was still sitting at the kitchen table. So, yeah, I'd have to say no to that one. I don't remember that being a problem for me before I was twelve. Or ever, really.

turns.doctor_question: Before age 12, did you often have trouble waiting your turn?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, waiting my turn? Yeah. Yes, definitely before twelve, just like the other things. But honestly, it's one of those things that has just never, ever gone away, so it's almost easier to think about how bad it is right now, because it's the exact same feeling I had when I was a kid waiting for the swings at recess. 

Like, I do a lot of UI/UX design, so I go to these weekend hackathons with the computer science kids, right? And the check-in lines on Friday nights are just... they are agonizing. I get really, really antsy waiting for my turn to just get my lanyard and get inside. I'll be standing there, and I catch myself constantly checking the time on my phone, like every thirty seconds, shifting my weight around, looking to see if the other lines are moving faster. It feels like my skin is crawling just from having to stand there and do nothing while other people take their time.

And it happens during office-hour queues, too. That might actually be worse. If I need help with a portfolio piece and there are, like, three people ahead of me waiting to talk to the professor, I am just a total mess out in the hallway. I get this overwhelming urge to just jump in before it’s actually my turn. I'll hear the person inside asking a question, and I'll think, "Oh my gosh, they are taking forever, let me just pop in and get my quick question answered," and I have to physically stop myself from barging through the door. I just want to jump in and get it over with. It's just this intense, physical impatience. I hate the feeling of being stalled or held up by other people's pacing. So, yeah, it definitely started when I was little, but it's still a massive issue for me literally every time I have to stand in a line.
